This Miscellaneous First Appeal is filed by respondents under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act,
1988 ('MV Act' for short), challenging the judgment and award passed by the Additional Senior Civil Judge and MACT XIII at Madhugiri in MVC No.124/2009, dated 15.09.2012.

entities.text: Additional Senior Civil Judge and MACT XIII at Madhugiri
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. For the sake of convenience, the parties herein are referred as per the ranks occupied by them before the Tribunal.

3. The brief factual matrix leading to the case are as under:
On 05.07.2009, at 3.00 p.m., deceased Nagaraju and his mother were working in their land for collecting the grass.
It is further alleged that at that time, respondent No.2 was tilling the land of Narasimaiah by means of power tiller.
While tilling the land, some grass got struck in the rotaries of the power tiller and respondent requested Nagaraju to remove the grass that was struck.

When Nagaraju was engaged in removing the grass from the rotaries of the power tiller, at that time, without directions or signals respondent No.2 in a negligent manner with high speed moved the power tiller as a result, the rotaries hit Nagaraj by causing fatal injuries.
He was shifted to Koratagere Hospital and then to Government Hospital, Tumkur and later on to Nimhans, Bangalore.
However, he succumbed because of the injuries on 09.07.2009.
The complaint was filed in this regard and the claimants being the legal heirs of the deceased Nagaraju filed the claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act.

Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22085281/
2 4.

entities.text: Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Respondents filed objections contending that the power tiller was never sent to the land of Narasimaiah.
Respondents have admitted that respondent No.2 was the driver of the power tiller.

However, there is a total denial of the accident by use of a power tiller and it is further asserted that MV Act is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case and hence, the claim came to be disputed.

5 . The Tribunal after appreciating the oral and documentary evidence, allowed the claim petition by awarding the compensation of Rs.4,52,000/- against respondents with interest at the rate of 6%
p.a., from the date of the petition.
This order is being challenged by the respondents before this Court.
6. Heard the learned counsel for the appellant and learned counsel for the respondents.
Perused the records.
7. The learned counsel for appellant has raised two defences.
His first defence is regarding the accident itself and his second defence is regarding provisions of the MV Act are not applicable.

He invites the attention of this Court to Section 2(28) of MV Act and contends that though a power tiller is a mechanically propelled vehicle, but there is no evidence to show that it is adapted for use on the road and accident has not occurred on a public road but it is in a private agricultural land.
He would also assert that there is no assertion regarding the power tiller being capable of adopting for use on a public road.

He would also assert that in a criminal case, respondent No.2 secures an acquittal and how the accident has occurred, there is no evidence and when the power tiller cannot be adapted for use on a road, the provisions of MV Act are not applicable.
Hence, he would contend that Tribunal has not considered any of these aspects and in a mechanical way, fastened the liability.
Hence, he would dispute the claim.
8. Per contra, the learned counsel for respondent/claimants would support the judgment and award passed by the tribunal.

He would contend that, as per Rule 2(v) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules,
the power tiller is defined and it is also capable of moving on a road.
He has also asserted that no specific defence is taken in the written statement regarding the non-applicability of provisions of the MV Act but a vague defence was set up.
He would also contend that the power tiller is capable of moving on the public road, as it is required to move from land to land for tilling.

He would also contend that since under the Central Motors Vehicles Rules itself power tiller is defined, it is evident that it is a motor vehicle and since it is capable of moving on a road in order to reach respective agricultural lands, it is adoptable to move on a public road.

He would also contend that it is also recognized under the Motor Vehicle Taxation Act, 1957 and in this regard, he invites attention of notification of the Central Government, dated 05.11.2004, issued under Section 41(4) of the MV Act regarding power tiller.
Hence, he would assert that the power tiller falls under the MV Act and hence, he would contend that the Tribunal is justified in awarding compensation and sought for dismissal of the appeal.

9. Having heard the arguments and perusing the records, now the following point would arise for my consideration:
Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22085281/
3

entities.text: Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "Whether the power tiller falls under the definition of the MV Act under Section 2(28)?"
10. It is evident that appellant No.1 is the owner of the power tiller and appellant No.2 is the driver of the power tiller.
This fact is undisputed.

The allegations of the claimants further disclose that on 05.07.2009, at 3.00 p.m., appellant No.2-Ramesh was tilling the land of one Narasimaiah by using power tiller and grass struck in the rotaries and as per his request, the deceased was removing the grass struck in rotaries and at that time, respondent No.2 moved the power tiller, which has resulted in the accident.
The records further disclose that a complaint was lodged in this regard immediately and FIR came to be issued.
This fact is evident from Ex.P2.
Ex.P3 is the inquest mahazar.
Though appellants have disputed the very accident itself, it is a fact that appellant No.2 was prosecuted in this regard and this fact is evident from Ex.R1.
Ex.R3 is the judgment, wherein appellant No.2 who was accused was acquitted.
But on perusal of the said judgment, it is evident that the acquittal was for lack of evidence, but it is not based on the fact that no accident has occurred or initiation of false case.
The judgment discloses that the incident did occur, but no honorary acquittal was granted to appellant No.2.
Hence, on the ground of acquittal, the learned counsel for appellants cannot argue that the accident as alleged never occurred.
11. Interestingly, appellant No.1 was got examined himself as RW1 and admittedly, he is not an eyewitness.
He denied the entire case.

However, during the cross- examination, when a suggestion was made that when deceased Nagaraju was requested by appellant No.2 to remove the grass struck in the rotaries, the deceased was removing the grass and when appellant No.2 moved the tiller, the accident has occurred, but he did not deny this aspect.
He asserts that the grass will not struck in the rotaries.
The learned counsel has produced a photograph of a tiller, but there is no evidence to show that this is the tiller involved in the accident.
He did not confront the same to the witnesses during the cross-examination.

Further, even on perusal of this tiller, the chain and engine were covered, but rotaries which are beneath are not all covered and possibility of strucking the grass when the wet mud is there cannot be ruled out.
Hence, the said arguments advanced by the learned counsel for appellant cannot be accepted.
12. Apart from that, the appellants have never challenged the prosecution and admittedly, appellant No.1 has got released the tiller from the custody of the Court, as admitted by him.
It is not his case that it was illegally seized by the police.
No such case is made out and appellant No.2 has not entered into witness box.
As such, the contention that the tiller was not involved in the accident cannot be accepted.

The Tribunal has appreciated the oral and documentary evidence in this regard and has rightly held that the tiller was involved in the accident and by use of the tiller itself this accident has occurred.
13.
The second ground urged by the appellants is that tiller does not fall under the definition of the MV Act and hence, the provisions of the MV Act are not applicable.
In this context, he invited the attention of the letter issued in the form of clarification regarding the registration of power tillers.
On perusal of this letter, it only discloses that power tillers are identified in two categories.
First category is exclusive use for agricultural land and second category is power tillers plying on the road with trailor.

But it is further clarified that the power tiller used for exclusive use of agricultural land Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22085281/
4 shall bear a warning sticker at a prominent location of the power tiller as to 'not for road use'.
This clarification was issued by Government of India Ministry of Road and Transport & Highways.

entities.text: Ministry of Road and Transport & Highways
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Hence, the intention of this letter clearly discloses that power tiller is a motor vehicle but having two different categories.
There is no evidence lead by respondent No.1 to show that his power tiller was having any warning, as referred in the letter referred above.
Hence, the contents of the said letter relied would not come to the aid of the appellant, but on the contrary, it would help the respondents-claimants.

14. The learned counsel for the appellant has further invited attention of the definitions under Section 2(28) of Motor Vehicle or vehicle which reads as under:
2(28) "motor vehicle" or "vehicle" means any mechanically propelled vehicle adapted for use upon roads whether the power of propulsion is transmitted thereto from an external or internal source and includes a chassis to which a body has not been attached and a trailer; but does not include a vehicle running upon fixed rails or a vehicle of a special type adapted for use only in a factory or in any other enclosed premises or a vehicle having less than four wheels fitted with engine capacity of not exceeding [twenty-five cubic centimetres];"
15.
On the basis of this definition, he would argue that though power tiller is a mechanical propelled vehicle, there is no evidence to show that it is adapted for use upon road.

At the same time,
admittedly, appellant No.1 is the owner of the power tiller and he should be having possession of all the records of power tiller as to its capacity.
In the entire evidence, he nowhere disclosed as to what is the engine capacity of the power tiller.
This material information is concealed by appellant No.1.
On the basis of this definition, he placed reliance on a decision of the Apex Court in 1974 SCC (2) 777 [Bolani Ores Ltd. Etc Vs. State Of Orissa Etc].

entities.text: 1974 SCC (2) 777 [Bolani Ores Ltd. Etc Vs. State Of Orissa Etc]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: But the facts and circumstances are entirely different and no doubt, in the said decision, the adoptability of the vehicle was considered but by material change, adoption is different and general adoption is entirely different.
The said principles will not come to the aid of the appellant in any way in view of the different facts and circumstance of the case in hand.
16. At this juncture only, it is relevant to consider the definition of power tiller as defined under the Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 1989.
Though power tiller is not defined under the main act, under the Rules, it is defined under the Rule 2(v).

Rule 2(v) defines power tiller which reads as under:
"(v) "Power tiller" means an agricultural machinery used for soil preparation having a single axle in which the direction of travel and its control for field operation is performed by the operator walking behind it.
This equipment may or may not have a riding attachment and when coupled to a trailer can be used for the transportation of goods.
The maximum speed of the power tiller when coupled to a trailer, shall not exceed 22km/h.
The maximum haulage capacity of the Power tiller coupled to a trailer shall not exceed 1.5 tons;]"

(Underlined by me)
Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22085281/
5 17.

entities.text: Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is further observed in this said definitions that it is basically used for soil preparation and its control for field operations is performed by the operator by working behind it.
It is further defined that this equipment may or may not have riding attachment and when coupled with the tiller, it can be used for transportation of the goods.
18. This definition of the power tiller under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 clarifies that power tiller is capable of adapting to public road for transportation.

Further, when the power tiller is required to be shifted from one land to other land, it is required to be moved and it is not the case of the appellants that they are required to shift it through a different vehicle.

It is having three wheels,
which is evident.

Hence, considering the definition of power tiller referred in Central Motor Vehicles Rules 2(v) coupled with the Motor Vehicles Act defined under Section 2(28) it is required to be treated as a motor vehicle as it is adoptable to the public road.

19. The learned counsel for the appellant has placed reliance on a decision reported in 2007 4 KarLJ 224 [The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd vs Sri D.Laxman S/o D.Thimmappa And....] This citation is not pertaining to a power tiller, but it was pertaining to a trailer attached to a tractor.
However, in view my observations above, as per the Rule 2(v) of the Central Motor Vehicle Rules, the propositions in the above cited decision will not come to the aid of the appellant in any way.

20. The learned counsel for appellant has further placed reliance on a full bench decision of this Court in Gadhilingappa @ Gadhilinga Vs. K. Guleppa S/o K Lingappa reported in ILR 2021 KAR 3377.
21.

entities.text: Gadhilingappa @ Gadhilinga Vs. K. Guleppa S/o K Lingappa reported in ILR 2021 KAR 3377
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the said decision, though incidentally considered the tractor and trailer, but again, it was not pertaining to the power tiller.
Apart from that, in the said decision, the defences available to the Insurance Company under Section 147 were considered and not regarding the power tiller.

Hence,
the said principles will not come to the aid of the appellants in any way.
22. He has further placed reliance on the unreported decision of the Bombay High Court in W.P.No.211/1999 (V.M.Salgaacar and Brothers vs State of Goa), dated 04.06.2008.

entities.text: W.P.No.211/1999 (V.M.Salgaacar and Brothers vs State of Goa)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: But again, the definitions of motor vehicles as defined under Section 2(28) was considered and drivers cabins were considered.
However, the said decision did not consider the definition of motor vehicle or power tiller under Rule 2(v) of Central Motor Vehicle Rules.
Hence, the said decision also will not come to the aid of the appellants in any way.

23. Considering the clarification issued by letter bearing No.35285/H3/2010, dated 13.08.2010 by Ministry of Road and Transports & Highways of Central Government, dated 24.05.2010, it is evident that a power tiller is a motor vehicle.

entities.text: Ministry of Road and Transports & Highways of Central Government
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Further, again this fact is clarified in view of the definition of power tiller given under the Central Motor Vehicle Rules.

The power tiller admittedly is having two/three wheels and it is required to move from field to field for tilling and the definition itself clarifies that it can be used for an attachment of trailer to use on road and thereby the adoptability of the said power tiller for to run on a public road is accepted.
Venkataswamy vs Venkatappa on 18 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22085281/
6 24.
On this point only the learned counsel for respondent placed reliance on a decision of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in LAWS(MPH)-2007-8-10/ACJ-2009-0- 1613 [Kusum vs. Kamal Kumar Soni].

In the said decision the Madhya Pradesh High Court has clearly held that power tiller is covered under the MV Act and claim was rightly filed before the MV Act and hence, the said principles are directly applicable to dispute involved in this case.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court has held that power tiller falls under MV Act and it is again consolidated by the Central Motor Vehicles Rules and clarification issued by the Ministry of Road Transports and Highways of Central Government.

entities.text: Ministry of Road Transports and Highways of Central Government
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Under such circumstances, the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the appellants that power tiller does not fall under the category of motor vehicle cannot be accepted at any stretch of imagination.
25. Admittedly, in the instant case, power tiller was not registered.

But at the same time,
non-registration of power tiller does not take it from the purview of the MV Act.
Further, the appellant has not disclosed the capacity of the engine and further, it is easily adaptable to the road as per the definition.
Apart from that, appellant No.1 has not put any warning board that it is not for movement on the road.
Considering these facts and circumstances, the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the appellant in this regard are not at all acceptable.

26. As regards quantum, there is no serious dispute between the parties and in view of these facts and circumstances, the point under consideration is answered in affirmative and as such, the appeal being devoid of any merits, needs to be dismissed.

Accordingly, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
(i) The appeal stands dismissed.
(ii) The statutory deposit if any made by the appellants shall be transmitted to the Tribunal.

Sd/-
